r: A condition is an expression that Python answers with True or False.
Comparison operators are ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=, plus in. Remember = stores, == asks.
Chaining such as 0 <= x <= 1 means "both comparisons are true".
Compare strings exactly, and compare computed floats with a tolerance.
if condition: runs its indented block only when the condition is True; else: runs when it is False.
The colon opens a block and indentation (four spaces) says which lines are inside it.
Exactly one branch of an if/else runs, then Python continues after it.
Read errors by their last line: expected ':', expected an indented block, unexpected indent, unindent does not match.
Any value can be used as a condition. Zero, empty things, None and False are falsy; everything else is truthy.
Truthiness checks emptiness, not meaning: "False" and "0" are truthy strings.
Use if items: to ask "is there anything in it?".
Use is None or is not None when 0 or an empty value is a legitimate answer.
and needs both sides True. or needs at least one. not flips the answer.
Precedence is not, then and, then or. Use parentheses to show your intent.
Write each comparison in full: x == 1 or x == 2, or use x in [1, 2].
Python evaluates and / or left to right and short-circuits: it stops once the answer is known.
Put the cheap or safe check on the left, for example count != 0 and total / count > 0.5.
and / or return one of their operands, so name or "anonymous" gives a default for an empty string.
Use elif for more than two roads. Python takes the first True branch and skips the rest.
Separate if statements are independent questions and can all run.
Put the strictest condition first. A wrong order runs without errors but gives wrong answers.
Nest an if only when the second question depends on the first, and flatten with and when you can.
A loop repeats a block so you write the instruction once.
for item in collection: visits every item in order; the indented block runs once per item (one iteration).
Trace a loop with a table of variable values per iteration.
An empty collection runs the block zero times, and the loop variable keeps its last value afterwards.
range(n) produces 0, 1, ..., n-1. range(a, b) produces a up to b-1. range(a, b, s) steps by s.
Start is included, stop is excluded. Count = stop - start when the step is 1.
A range that cannot reach the stop is empty, not an error.
Off-by-one errors: to include the last number, add 1 to the stop.
Most loops build an answer: set a starting value before the loop, update it inside, read it after.
Accumulator total += x, counter n += 1 under an if, flag found = True, best-so-far with float("inf") as the initial minimum.
Initialise outside the loop. Inside the loop it resets each time; missing altogether it raises NameError.
while condition: tests the condition before every round and repeats while it is True.
The block must change something the condition depends on, otherwise the loop cannot end.
If the condition is False at the start, the block runs zero times.
Use and in the condition to add a second reason to stop, such as an epoch limit.
A while loop that never makes its condition False is an infinite loop.
Causes: not updating, updating the wrong way, or a != test that gets skipped over.
Stop a runaway with Ctrl+C in a terminal; reload the page here. Better: add a maximum-rounds limit to the condition.
Use for when you have data or a known count, and while when you repeat until something happens.
continue skips the rest of this round, and the loop carries on with the next item.
break leaves the loop immediately; nothing after it in the block runs, and the remaining items are never visited.
Both are usually inside an if, so they trigger only on a special case.
In a while loop, update the counter before continue, or the loop may never end.
A nested loop puts one loop in the block of another. The inner loop runs completely for every round of the outer loop.
Total runs = outer count x inner count.
break and continue affect only the innermost loop.
Use distinct names for the loop variables, such as row and col.
enumerate(items) gives (position, item) pairs; start=1 changes the first number.
zip(a, b) walks two lists in parallel, pair by pair, and stops at the shorter one.
Write for i, (p, t) in enumerate(zip(a, b)) when you need both, with names shaped like the data.
Unpacking a, b = pair splits a pair into two names.
A comprehension builds a new list in one line: [expression for item in source if test].
It is the same recipe as a loop with append. Read it aloud as English.
Front part = transform, if at the end = filter, a if c else b at the front = choose between two values.
{key: value for ...} builds a dictionary. Keep a plain loop when the body gets complicated.
[...] builds a list, {...} (no colon) builds a set that removes duplicates, (...) builds a lazy generator.
Use sorted(a_set) for a predictable print order.
A generator hands out values on demand, saves memory with sum, max and friends, and can be used only once.
In a nested comprehension the for parts go in the same order as the nested loops: outer first.
The else of a for loop runs only if the loop finished without a break. It replaces the "found" flag in searches.
The else must line up with for. Under the if it means something different.
:= (walrus) assigns a value and uses it in one expression, for example if (n := len(x)) > 3:.
Both tools are optional; use them when they make code shorter and clearer.

r: Copy-pasted logic must be fixed in every copy, hides the intent of the program, and has no name.
The rule is DRY: keep each piece of logic in exactly one place.
A function is a named block of code. You write it once and call it as often as you like, like a recipe card you reuse with different ingredients.
A function is a machine: inputs go in, the body runs, an output comes back.
def name(parameters): followed by an indented body defines a function and runs nothing.
name(...) calls it. Without the parentheses you only refer to the function.
A call before the definition gives NameError: name '...' is not defined.
Parameters are the names in the def line; arguments are the values in the call.
Positional arguments match by order; keyword arguments (name=value) match by name and can come in any order, but only after all positional ones.
A call that does not fit the definition fails with a TypeError that names the function and the parameter, or with a SyntaxError for positional-after-keyword.
Each call creates a frame holding that call's own parameters and variables; frames are stacked, and only the top one runs.
When a function returns, its frame is thrown away and Python resumes exactly where the call was made.
A traceback is the call stack printed out: read it from the bottom (the error) upwards (who called whom).
return value ends the function and hands the value back to the caller; the call then acts as that value.
print only displays. A function without return gives back None, which causes NoneType errors later.
Several return lines are fine, because only one runs. return a, b gives back a tuple you can unpack.
Make sure every path through a function returns something.
name=value in a definition makes a parameter optional; defaulted parameters go after required ones.
A default is created once, when def runs, so a list default is shared between calls. Use None and create the list in the body.
*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.
A star in a call (f(*items)) does the reverse and spreads a collection into separate arguments.
Variables assigned inside a function are local: they exist only during the call.
Python looks names up in the order Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.
Reading a global works; assigning to a name makes it local unless you declare global name.
Prefer passing arguments in and returning results out; avoid global and never reuse names like sum or list.
Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem.
Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls, and a recursive case that moves toward it.
Each call has its own frame, so the calls do not confuse each other; the answers come back in reverse order.
With no reachable base case Python raises RecursionError after about a thousand calls.
lambda params: expression builds a small anonymous function whose expression value is returned automatically.
Its main use is as the key for sorted, max and min, which call it on each item.
A lambda can only contain one expression. Use def for anything larger.
A docstring is a triple-quoted string as the first line of a function body; read it with help(f) or f.__doc__.
Type hints (x: int, -> float, -> None) document the inputs and output but are never enforced by Python.
Together they let a function explain itself to you, your teammates, and your tools.
A function can return a function. The inner function remembers variables from the outer one: a closure.
Each call of the outer function makes a separate set of remembered variables.
To reassign a remembered variable from the inner function, declare it nonlocal.
partial(f, ...) builds a simpler function with some arguments already filled in.
reduce(f, items) folds a sequence into one value by combining pairs.
@lru_cache makes a function remember its answers, which is a big saving for repeated calls, especially recursion.
import module gives access via module.name; from module import name gives the bare name; as renames.
The standard library is a big set of modules: math, random, datetime, collections and many more.
random.seed(n) makes random numbers repeatable, which matters for reproducible experiments.
A missing import causes NameError; a wrong name inside a real module causes ImportError.
A module is a .py file; import finds it via sys.modules and sys.path, runs it once and gives you a module object.
Your own folder is searched first: never name your files after standard modules.
__name__ is "__main__" when a file runs directly and the module name when imported, so if __name__ == "__main__": guards script-only code.
A folder of modules with an __init__.py is a package.

r: A collection holds many values under one name, so code does not depend on how many values there are.
Python has four built-in collections: list, tuple, dict and set.
Ordered means items have positions; mutable means the collection can be changed after it is created.
len(collection) counts the items; sum(list) adds a list of numbers.
An index is a position counted from 0; negative indexes count from the end (-1 is the last).
A valid index for a list of length n runs from -n to n - 1; anything else raises IndexError.
A slice [start:stop:step] builds a new list and excludes the stop position.
Slices never raise IndexError and never change the original list.
Methods that change a list (append, sort, remove, ...) return None, so never assign their result.
sorted(x) returns a new sorted list; x.sort() reorders x itself.
append adds one item, extend adds each item of another list.
remove of a missing value raises ValueError; pop on an empty list raises IndexError. Check with in or if items: first.
A variable is a name tag on an object, and b = a puts a second tag on the same object.
With mutable objects this is aliasing: changing through one name shows through the other. is tests for it.
Make an independent list with .copy(), list(x) or x[:].
Copies are shallow: inner collections are still shared. Use copy.deepcopy when you need full independence.
A tuple is an ordered, immutable collection written with (); indexing and slicing work like a list.
Assigning to a tuple item raises TypeError.
A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,).
Unpacking (x, y = pair) splits a tuple or list into names by position, and the counts must match or you get a ValueError.
A dict stores key: value pairs and looks values up by key, written d[key].
d[key] = v adds a new pair or replaces the value of an existing key.
del d[key] and d.pop(key) remove a pair; pop returns the value.
key in d tests keys only; reading a missing key raises KeyError, and a duplicate key silently keeps the last value.
d.get(key, default) reads without ever raising KeyError; the default is None if you omit it.
A for loop over a dict yields keys; use .values() for values and .items() for (key, value) pairs.
Do not add or remove keys while looping over the same dict.
Keys must be hashable (immutable): strings, numbers and tuples work; lists, dicts and sets do not.
A set stores each value once and has no order or positions; make an empty one with set(), not {}.
add inserts, discard removes safely, remove raises KeyError if the value is missing.
in on a set is fast because it uses hashing; a list has to check items one by one.
& intersection, | union, - difference, ^ in exactly one, <= subset. Print with sorted(...) for a stable order.
Choose by the question you will ask: position (list), fixed record (tuple), lookup by label (dict), membership and uniqueness (set).
You can convert between them: dict(pairs), list(d), set(items), tuple(items).
Mixing shapes is normal: lists of dicts and dicts of lists appear everywhere in real data.
A list of dicts is a dataset: each dict is a record and each key is a column.
records[i]["field"] first picks a record by position, then a field by key.
sorted cannot compare dicts; pass key= with a function that returns the value to compare.
A lambda is an unnamed one-line function. max, min and sorted all accept key=lambda ....
Collections nest: dicts hold lists, lists hold dicts, dicts hold dicts. JSON is that same shape written as text.
Read a chain like d["a"][0]["b"] left to right, one step at a time; use a key for a dict and an index for a list.
TypeError: list indices must be integers means you used a key on a list; a KeyError usually means the wrong level.
json.loads(text) turns JSON text into Python data and json.dumps(obj) turns it back into text.
Counter(items) counts occurrences; .most_common(n) lists the top n as (item, count) tuples.
defaultdict(list) creates an empty list for any missing key, which removes the if key not in d guard when grouping.
namedtuple gives a tuple named fields (record.score) and stays immutable.
All three come from from collections import ....
first, *rest = items gives the leftovers to the starred name, always as a list (possibly empty); only one star is allowed.
[*a, *b] builds a list from two lists, and f(*items) passes items as separate arguments.
{**a, **b} merges dicts into a new one; on a clash the later dict wins.
Merging copies only one layer: inner collections are still shared.
A comprehension is [value for item in source if condition]; the brackets decide the result: [...] list, {k: v ...} dict, {x ...} set.
Loop over d.items() to get key and value together; a bare for k, v in d fails with a ValueError.
Round brackets around a comprehension make a generator: handy inside sum or any, not for printing.
If a comprehension gets hard to read, use a normal loop.

r: Classes, inheritance, dunder methods, properties, dataclasses and unittest are taught in the OOP track. This chapter uses them but does not re-teach them.
Real data lives in files and is often messy, so a real program must expect failure at every step.
Errors are objects made from classes in a family tree; __mro__ shows a class and its parents.
This chapter covers reading errors, catching them, raising them, then files, paths, CSV and JSON.
A traceback lists the active function calls, oldest at the top and newest at the bottom.
Read it from the bottom: the last line gives the error type and message, the last File line gives where Python was when it failed.
The place where Python noticed the problem is not always the place where the mistake lives; follow the calls upwards to find out who passed in the bad value.
The common types: ValueError, TypeError, IndexError, KeyError, ZeroDivisionError, NameError.
try: runs risky code; if an error is raised, Python skips the rest of the block and looks for a matching except.
Name the error you expect: except ValueError:. A handler never catches a type it does not name.
except ValueError as e gives you the error object; printing e shows Python's own explanation.
A bare except: hides real bugs. Keep the try block small so the handler matches what you meant.
else runs when the try block finished without an error; finally runs always, last, even around return.
Several except clauses are checked from the top, and the first match wins.
Error types form a family tree; catching a parent (like OSError or ValueError) catches its children too.
Order handlers from most specific to most general.
Validate at the door: raise an error with a clear message instead of letting bad data travel.
raise stops the current function; the error goes up through the callers until a matching except catches it.
Subclass a built-in error (class ScoreError(ValueError): pass) to get a precise type, optionally with extra attributes.

Replacing one error by another can hide the real cause; raise NewError(...) from e keeps it as __cause__.

Without from, Python still shows the original, but as "during handling of the above exception, another exception occurred".
from None deliberately hides an original that would only confuse.
Files let data outlive the program. open(name, mode) returns a file object; 'r' reads (the default), 'w' writes.
Always use with open(...) as f:; the file is closed for you when the block ends, even after an error.
write adds no newline, so put \n in the text where you want a line to end.
Common errors: ValueError: I/O operation on closed file. and FileNotFoundError. Files on this page live in an in-memory file system that resets on reload.
'r' reads, 'w' erases and writes, 'a' appends, 'x' refuses to overwrite; adding 'b' gives bytes.
A file has a cursor: each read moves it forward, so a second read() gives '' until you seek(0).
Loop over the file object to read line by line; use .strip() to remove the newline.
write needs a string and adds no newline; print(..., file=f) adds one.
A file holds bytes; an encoding such as UTF-8 turns characters into bytes and back. Reader and writer must agree.
UnicodeDecodeError means the bytes did not fit the encoding you named. Fix it by naming the correct encoding, not by ignoring the problem.
Always pass encoding='utf-8' for text files you share.
In text mode Python translates line endings; newline='' turns that off, which the csv module needs.
splitlines() or iterating the file avoids the empty last item that split('\n') leaves.
A Path object replaces string juggling: build with /, inspect with .name, .stem, .suffix, .parent.
write_text, read_text, mkdir, exists, glob and iterdir cover most everyday file work.
Wrap glob/iterdir in sorted when order matters, and use mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) before writing into a new folder.
Path works anywhere a file name string does, including open().
csv.reader gives lists, csv.DictReader gives dictionaries keyed by the header, and csv.DictWriter writes them back.
Every CSV value is a string; convert it yourself and guard the conversion with try/except ValueError.
Open CSV files with newline='' (and encoding='utf-8').

JSON is nested data as text: objects become dicts, arrays become lists, true/false/null become True/False/None.
dumps/loads work with strings; dump/load work with open files. Use indent=2 for readable output.

Use .get(key, default) when a key may be missing.
with calls __enter__ at the start and __exit__ at the end, even after an error.
Files are context managers, so with open(...) closes them for you.
__exit__ returning False lets errors continue; True would hide them.

Data problems: ValueError (unusable content), KeyError (missing name), TypeError (wrong kind), UnicodeDecodeError (wrong encoding), JSONDecodeError (bad JSON).

Group related errors under one base class: except Parent catches every child too.

def creates a function object; the name is only a label. f refers to it, f() runs it.
A function can be passed to another function and returned from one.
These are the two ingredients of a decorator: something that takes a function, and something that hands a function back.
'NoneType' object is not callable usually means stray parentheses or a missing return.
An inner function can use variables from the function around it.

Each call of the outer function builds a new inner function with its own backpack.

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapper function; @name above a def means f = name(f).
Decoration time happens once, when the def is read. Call time happens on every call and goes through the wrapper.
The wrapper uses *args, **kwargs to accept anything and must return the original's result.

Without help, a decorated function's __name__ and __doc__ become those of wrapper.
Put @wraps(func) (from functools) on the wrapper to copy the original's identity; __wrapped__ reaches the original.
Stacked decorators apply bottom-up, so the top decorator is the outermost layer.
@name(args) first calls name(args), then applies whatever it returns to the function below.

Decoration steps happen once at definition time; only the wrapper runs on each call.
TypeError: ... missing 1 required positional argument: 'func' means the parentheses do not match the design: add them, or remove them.
A generator function contains yield; calling it returns a generator object and runs nothing yet.
yield hands out a value and pauses the function; the next next() resumes right after it.
Reaching the end raises StopIteration, which for loops catch to stop cleanly.
A generator holds one value at a time (memory-friendly), is used up after one pass, and cannot be indexed or measured with len().
A generator can filter and repair as it goes: yield for good items, try/except around the bad ones.

(expression for x in data) is a lazy generator expression; [...] builds the whole list.
Laziness saves memory and lets you stop early, but the result is single-use.
A level says how important a message is: DEBUG 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30, ERROR 40, CRITICAL 50.
The threshold (level= in basicConfig) hides everything below it, with no code edited.

Use logging.exception(...) inside except to keep the traceback.

r: A command-line program is started from a terminal, and extra words after its name are arguments.
Python hands those words to your script as the list sys.argv; item 0 is the script name and every item is a string.
Reading sys.argv by hand means converting types yourself and crashing with unhelpful errors when something is missing. argparse (next) solves both.
An argparse parser is a description of the arguments you accept: create it, call add_argument for each one, then call parse_args.
parse_args(list) returns a Namespace; each flag becomes an attribute, with the dashes dropped.
type=, default= and required= handle conversion, fallbacks and mandatory values, and bad input produces a readable usage message plus exit code 2.
action="store_true" makes an on/off switch that is False unless present; --some-flag becomes args.some_flag.
choices= restricts a value to a fixed list, and help= text becomes the automatic --help page.
Wrap parsing in main(argv=None) so you can test with a list now and read the real command line later.
A Path is an object that understands its own pieces: .name, .stem, .suffix, .parent, .parts.
Join with /, never with + or manual slashes; it works on every operating system.
File actions live on the Path: .exists(), .mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True), .read_text(), .write_text(), .glob().
JSON is the standard text spelling of dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and null, so different programs can exchange data.
json.dumps(obj) turns Python into JSON text; json.loads(text) turns JSON text back into Python objects (the s means string).
Bad text raises JSONDecodeError; unsupported Python types raise TypeError; missing keys raise KeyError.
HTTP is one request (method, URL, headers, optional body) answered by one response (status code, headers, body).
A URL has a scheme, host, path and optional ?name=value query parameters; urllib.parse can split one.
Read the status code before the body: 2xx success, 4xx your request was wrong, 5xx the server had trouble.
requests.get(url, params=..., timeout=...) performs the HTTP conversation and returns a Response with .status_code, .text, .json() and .raise_for_status().
Always set a timeout, and call raise_for_status() so 4xx/5xx errors stop the script where they happen.
Practise the parsing side against a small fake response class; the code behaves the same with the real library.
POST sends data to create something; json= builds the JSON body and its Content-Type header.
Authentication is usually a token in the Authorization: Bearer ... header, never in the URL.
Branch on the status code (201, 401, 400, ...), and retry only temporary 5xx/429 failures, with a fixed limit.
A process is a running program; subprocess.run starts a child process and returns returncode, stdout and stderr.
Return code 0 means success. A failure does not raise unless you use check=True.
Pass commands as a list, never build a shell=True string from user input: that is command injection.
An environment variable is a named text setting supplied by whoever starts the program; os.environ reads it like a dict.
Use .get(name, default) for optional settings and fail with a clear message for required secrets.
Values are always strings: convert numbers with int() and compare booleans against words like "true".
Slow I/O makes scripts wait; asyncio lets one worker keep several tasks in progress by switching whenever one is waiting.
async def makes a coroutine function; calling it gives a coroutine object, and await is what actually runs it.
The event loop is the scheduler that runs whichever task is ready. Forgetting await or using it outside async def are the two classic errors.
asyncio.gather(a, b, c) runs coroutines concurrently and returns their results in the order you passed them, not the order they finished.
asyncio.create_task(coro) starts work immediately and returns a handle that you await later.
Real scripts start the loop once with asyncio.run(main()); this browser console lets you write await main() directly.
By default one failing task makes gather raise. Add return_exceptions=True to get errors back as list items, and test them with isinstance(r, Exception).
asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout) puts a time limit on a wait and raises TimeoutError when it is exceeded.
Never block inside async def. async for and async with are the same ideas as for and with when each step may wait.

The DRY rule (Don't Repeat Yourself) says every idea should live in one place.
Three near-identical classes (Dog, Cat, Bird) differ only in their sound, yet copy-paste repeats everything else.
Inheritance lets a class reuse another class's code; class Dog(Animal) gives Dog everything Animal has.
Read tracebacks from the bottom line upward: the last line names the error, the lines above show where it happened.
The is-a test ("a Dog is an Animal") decides whether inheritance makes sense.
class Dog(Animal) makes Animal the parent (base class, superclass) and Dog the child (subclass).
The child receives every attribute and method of the parent automatically; there is no copying, only a search that moves up the tree.
Children may add methods; parents never receive them.
isinstance(obj, Class) respects families; type(obj) == Class does not. issubclass(A, B) compares two classes.
If a child defines __init__, Python uses it and does not run the parent's automatically.
super().__init__(...) calls the parent's __init__ on the same object; call it first in the child's __init__.
The trace: create empty object, child __init__ starts, parent __init__ fills in its attributes, control returns, child adds its own.
AttributeError: 'Dog' object has no attribute 'name' after a custom __init__ usually means super().__init__ is missing.
Do not pass self to super().__init__; do pass every argument the parent needs.
Overriding: define a method with the same name in the child; Python finds the child's first.
Extending: override, and call super().method(...) to keep the parent's behaviour and add to it. This avoids copying the parent's code.
The parent's version still exists; super() or Parent.method(obj, ...) reaches it.
Typos silently create a new method instead of overriding; check spelling when an override does not run.
Keep the same parameters, remember return, and use super() rather than self when you mean the parent.
Polymorphism ("many forms"): different objects respond to the same method name, each in its own way.
Python picks the version to run by looking at the object's own class at the moment of the call (dynamic dispatch).
It replaces long if/elif chains and lets you add new kinds without touching the calling code.
You already use it: len(), + and print() behave differently for different types.
Keep every version's inputs and return values consistent, or the caller cannot treat them alike.
Duck typing: care about what an object can do, not what family it belongs to.
Unrelated classes can take part in polymorphism if they share method names.
hasattr checks for an ability first (LBYL); calling and catching AttributeError is the other style (EAFP).
Python's own tools (len, for, in) use duck typing through special methods.
Use isinstance at boundaries and for Python's built-in kinds; avoid it for choosing behaviour among your own classes.
Multi-level inheritance: a child can itself be a parent; features pass down every generation.
The MRO (method resolution order) is the list of classes Python searches: the object, then its class, parents in order, then object.
The first match wins; later classes are not consulted. Print it with ClassName.__mro__.
super() means "the next class in the MRO", so super() calls can chain up through several levels.
Instance attributes hide class attributes; every level with an __init__ must call super().__init__.
Multiple inheritance: class Duck(A, B, C) gives the child every parent's abilities.
A mixin is a small, single-purpose class made to be mixed into others, not used alone.
The first-listed parent wins when names collide; put mixins before the main base class.
The diamond problem: the MRO lists each class once, children before parents, respecting your left-to-right order.
super() means "the next class in the MRO", so use it consistently; avoid multiple inheritance when parents overlap heavily.
An abstract base class (class X(ABC)) is a contract: it lists methods (@abstractmethod) that children must write.
You cannot create an object from an abstract class, or from a child that leaves a required method unfinished; Python raises TypeError at creation time.
Ordinary methods in the ABC are still shared by all children.
Liskov substitution: any child must work wherever the parent is expected; a child that refuses a parent's promise signals a bad design.
Inheritance is a strong link. When the is-a test fails or the child does not want all the parent's methods, use composition (OOP Part 4).

frozen=True makes fields read-only (FrozenInstanceError) and lets the object be a dict key or set member.
order=True adds <, > and sorting, comparing fields in the order they are written.
__post_init__ runs right after the generated __init__: use it to validate or to compute derived fields (field(init=False)).
asdict gives a plain dictionary; replace gives a modified copy and leaves the original alone.
Dataclasses suit "holders of facts". Normal classes suit objects that mostly do work and hide their insides.

A type hint is a label (name: str, -> float) that tells readers and tools what kind of value is expected.
Read list[X] as "a list of X" and X | None as "an X, or nothing".

Editors and checkers such as mypy use hints to warn you before you run the program.

Tell, don't ask: call a method such as order.pay() and let the object enforce its own rules, instead of checking its data from outside.

A CRC card (Class, Responsibility, Collaborators) is a tiny table for one class.
Give every rule exactly one owner, so it is stored and enforced in one place.
Define classes before use, and do not create classes that have no job.
Build in stages: add one small piece, run it, print something, then move on. A failure points at the last thing you added.

raise LibraryError(...) refuses an action, and try / except catches the refusal so the program can carry on.
Check every rule first, change state last, so a refusal leaves no half-done work.
Read a traceback from its last line. A missing argument, a missing self. and text used as a number each have a very recognisable message.
Checking by eye does not scale; a test writes the expected answer down once and lets the computer compare.
A unittest test is a method starting with test in a class that inherits unittest.TestCase.
Output: ok per test, then Ran N tests and OK or FAILED. A FAIL is a wrong answer, an ERROR is a crash.
setUp gives every test a fresh object; assertRaises checks that an error is raised; assertAlmostEqual handles decimals.

Test behaviour through public methods, not internal attributes, so you can change the insides safely.
One idea per test, with a name that reads like a sentence. Use subTest for tables of similar cases.

Replace the outside world (email, files, clocks) with a small fake that is passed in.

Names are arrows: two names can point at one list. Most of these bugs are that one fact in disguise.
Put per-object lists in __init__, copy lists you receive, and use None instead of [] as a default.

Do not change a list while looping over it, do not let methods bounce between two objects forever, and keep inheritance shallow.

Functions that all take the same object as their first argument usually want to become methods of that object's class.
Thin wrappers keep old callers and old tests working while you move code; remove them at the end.
A small step plus an immediate test run makes a slip easy to find.
JSON only understands basic types, so give classes to_dict() and a from_dict() classmethod.
Saving turns objects into text; loading builds new objects with the same facts. Arrows between objects become names or ids.
Each class packs and unpacks only its own level and delegates the rest to the classes it holds.
Validate incoming data and raise clear errors. Put except blocks for the more specific error first.
Never load pickle data you did not create: loading can run arbitrary code. Prefer JSON.
Read an unfamiliar class in this order: attributes (vars), public methods (dir filtered), special methods, base classes, docs.
help(), docstrings and inspect.signature show what the author documented, without opening the source.

r: A log is a diary a program writes: one line of text per event, appended in time order.
Engineers read logs because a live production system cannot be paused and inspected; the log is the only witness.
Almost every log question is one of four: what happened, when, how often, to whom.
A log analysis has four stages: the program writes, the file stores, your script reads and summarises, and you get an answer.
A log line has a format: fields in a fixed order, separated by spaces, with quotes and brackets around fields that contain spaces.
nginx access lines carry IP, time, request, status code, bytes, referrer, user agent and request time. sshd lines carry a timestamp, host, program and a free-text event.
split() is quick, but fixed positions silently break when a field contains spaces or is missing.
Better plan: describe a field by its surroundings (a pattern), which is what regular expressions are for.
.read() and .readlines() load the whole file into memory; for line in f reads one line at a time.
A generator function uses yield: it hands back one value, pauses, and resumes on the next request.
Chaining generators builds a lazy pipeline where memory depends on one item, not the whole file.
A generator is single-use (a second pass gives nothing) and has no len().
A regex describes the shape of text. re.search finds the first fit (or None); re.findall lists all fits.
Literals match themselves. Classes (\d, \s, \w, [abc], [^"], .) match ONE character from a set.
Quantifiers (+, *, ?, {n}) say how many times; anchors like $ match positions.
Escape a literal dot as \., and write every pattern as a raw string r"...".
Parentheses capture pieces. Named groups (?P<name>...) let you read m["name"] or m.groupdict().
Greedy quantifiers take as much as possible and back off. Lazy (*?) takes as little as possible. A negated class such as [^"]* is the precise choice.
| means or, (?:...)? makes a chunk optional, and re.VERBOSE with comments makes long patterns readable. Compile once with re.compile.
A failed match is None; check for it before using the result. Know when to use match, search, fullmatch.
Regex groups return strings. Convert to int and float once, at the edge, and keep real types afterwards.
A dataclass is a named-field record: a tidy row with typed fields.
A production parser returns None for garbage, counts it, and continues. Convert the log's - ("no value") deliberately.
The skipped ratio is a health signal; alert when it jumps.
Top-N questions are "count each item, then rank". A plain dict raises KeyError on a missing key; Counter treats it as 0.
.most_common(n) returns the top n as (item, count) pairs.
Normalise before you count, for example by removing the query string.
Memory grows with distinct keys, not lines. Gather several counters in one pass.
Log timestamps are text. strptime(text, format) makes a real datetime, and strftime turns one back into a label such as an hour bucket.
The UTC offset tells you how a local clock relates to UTC. Convert to UTC early with .astimezone(timezone.utc).

First question for any slow program: is it I/O-bound or CPU-bound?
Concurrency on CPU-bound work gives no speedup; more workers than waits also gives none.
A deterministic tick simulation makes scheduling behaviour visible and repeatable, and the rest of this chapter uses it.
The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time; it is released during blocking I/O and in many C libraries.
CPU-bound pure-Python threads do not scale; I/O-bound threads do; processes sidestep the GIL at the cost of copying data.
The GIL protects the interpreter's internals, not your invariants: x += 1 is several steps.
Free-threaded builds (3.13 experimental, 3.14 supported, optional) remove the lock but not the need for locks in your own code.
Choose by the task's profile: waits go to asyncio or threads, pure-Python compute goes to processes, array maths goes to numpy.
Threads are pre-emptive and share memory; processes copy data and dodge the GIL; coroutines switch only at await.
Every option needs a limit (pool size, semaphore) tied to what the downstream system can handle.

A race is a result that depends on timing. Check-then-act and read-modify-write are its two most common shapes.
Controlling the interleaving (generators plus an explicit schedule) turns a heisenbug into a reproducible test.
Enumerating all orderings shows how many are bad; the real-world probability is small but never zero.
The cure is to make check and act one indivisible step: a lock, an atomic operation, or a conditional update.
A lock makes a critical section behave like one step, and with lock: is the safe way to use it.
Deadlock needs a cycle of waiting; a global lock order removes cycles.
Keep critical sections short, avoid calling unknown code under a lock, and add timeouts so hangs become visible.
Exhaustive schedule enumeration turns "seems fine" into "proved for this case".
A queue passes messages between workers so they share nothing else, and the queue does the locking.
Producers and consumers run at their own pace; the queue absorbs bursts.
Shut down with one sentinel per consumer, and always call task_done() in a finally.
Delivery across machines is usually at-least-once, so pair queues with idempotent handlers.
A timeout is ambiguous: the work may or may not have happened, so retries must be safe.
Idempotency keys turn non-idempotent operations into safe ones: generate once, store result per key, reject mismatched reuse, insert the key atomically.
Retry only transient errors, with capped exponential backoff plus jitter, a maximum attempt count and an overall deadline.
Retries multiply across layers (3 layers of 3 attempts each = 27x); retry in one place and budget them.
A coroutine is a paused function; a task schedules it; the event loop runs ready tasks and sleeps until the next timer or ready socket.
await pauses the current task only when the awaited thing has to wait. That pause is the only time other tasks run.
await a(); await b() is sequential; gather or create_task makes tasks concurrent.
Keep references to tasks, never call asyncio.run inside a running loop, and treat "never awaited" warnings as bugs.
Never block inside a coroutine: use async libraries or offload with an executor; debug mode reports slow callbacks.
Cancellation is an exception at the current await: clean up in finally and re-raise CancelledError.
Put a timeout on every outbound call, or a deadline on the whole operation.
Prefer TaskGroup to gather for structured concurrency; await between check and act still allows races.
Unbounded queues turn overload into slow collapse (growing memory and latency); bound every queue.
When full, choose deliberately: block, shed (429/503) or spill/scale.
Little's Law (L = lambda x W) links in-flight work, throughput and latency; semaphores and pool sizes are how you cap in-flight work.
Latency explodes as utilisation approaches 100 percent, so leave headroom and watch queue depth and oldest-item age.
Profile first: timeit for snippets, cProfile for call-level cost, tracemalloc for memory, py-spy for live processes.
Read the table: high tottime with few calls means an expensive algorithm; high ncalls means call less; high cumtime with low tottime means look at the callees.
In a flame graph, wide boxes with nothing above them are the hotspot; left-to-right order carries no meaning.
Use minimums of repeated runs, realistic data, and relative rather than absolute numbers.

r: A threat model lists assets, attackers, data flows and trust boundaries, then asks what could go wrong at each crossing.
STRIDE gives six prompts: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege.
Risk is likelihood times impact; sort, fix the top, and record every accepted risk with a name and date.
Untrusted data can ride inside a trusted arrow, so inspect what your code builds from it.
The OWASP Top 10 is a ranked map of common web risks; learn the themes, since names and order change by edition.
Read each request left to right and ask which theme could bite at each stage.
Scanners find patterns quickly but have false positives and false negatives; review and tests still matter.
Fail closed: when you cannot prove access is allowed, deny it.
SQL injection happens when untrusted text is pasted into SQL, so data changes the query's meaning.
UNION injection turns any injectable field into a way to read other tables.
Fix by parameterizing every query; never rely on filtering or escaping quotes.
Identifiers and sort order cannot be parameters: use an allowlist. Keep payload regression tests.
Any time you build a string for another interpreter (shell, path, eval), untrusted text can become instructions.
Avoid the shell: pass argument lists; validate with a strict pattern; quote with shlex.quote as a last resort; use -- to stop option injection.
For paths: normalize, then check the result is inside the base folder by whole segments.
Never eval or unpickle untrusted data. Use an AST allowlist for expressions and JSON for data.
A hash is a one-way fingerprint; attackers do not reverse it, they guess and compare.
Fast hashes such as SHA-256 let attackers test billions of guesses per second, and unsalted ones expose duplicates.
A unique random salt per password defeats shared tables but does not slow guessing.
Use a deliberately slow, salted password hash (scrypt, bcrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2) with a cost you can raise.
Store one self-describing record: algorithm, cost, salt, hash. Use a library (Argon2id or bcrypt) when you can; PBKDF2 or scrypt from hashlib otherwise.
Compare secrets with hmac.compare_digest, not ==.
Upgrade weak records at login; you can never upgrade them without the password.
Throttle online guessing, keep error messages generic, and add MFA for valuable accounts.
A session id is a bearer ticket: whoever holds it is logged in. Generate it with secrets, at least 128 bits.
Rotate the id at login to defeat fixation; expire on idle, absolute time and logout, all enforced server-side.
Set HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and a bounded Max-Age, and check the real header.
Never use counters, timestamps, hashes of user names, or random for identifiers that guard access.
A JWT is signed, not encrypted: header.payload.signature, all base64url text.
The verifier chooses the accepted algorithms. Never trust alg from the token; reject none and pin one algorithm per key.
A valid signature is not enough: check exp, nbf, iss and aud as well.
Use a maintained library for real work; this section shows what it must do for you.
Use short-lived access tokens plus rotating single-use refresh tokens; a replayed old refresh token signals theft.
Stateless tokens cannot be recalled: use a denylist by jti or a per-user token version when you need instant revocation.
localStorage is readable by injected scripts; HttpOnly cookies are not, but need CSRF defences.
Choose sessions or JWTs by your revocation and scaling needs, not by fashion.
Authentication says who you are; authorization says what you may touch. Missing object-level checks (IDOR/BOLA) are the most common serious API bug.
Check ownership in the lookup itself, and return the same 404 for "not yours" and "does not exist".
Random ids reduce guessing but never replace an access check.
RBAC maps roles to permissions; default deny; enforce on the server, never only in the interface.
ABAC decides from attributes of user, resource and context; keep the policy in one function and test its boundaries.
Tenant isolation: the tenant comes from the session, every query filters on it, and a scoped repository (plus row-level security) makes forgetting impossible.
Mass assignment lets clients set fields you never meant to expose: allowlist the editable and returned fields.
Test authorization as a matrix of users by resources.
SSRF makes your server fetch a URL the attacker chose, borrowing its privileged network position.
Text blocklists fail because one address has many spellings; validate the parsed, resolved IP address.
Parse, allow scheme and host, resolve once, require a public address, pin the connection, re-check redirects.
Add network-level and permission-level defence: isolated fetchers, hardened metadata service, least-privilege keys.
XSS runs attacker script in your page: encode output for its context, avoid innerHTML-style escape hatches, add CSP and HttpOnly cookies.
CSRF rides the browser's automatic cookies: use SameSite plus anti-forgery tokens for state-changing requests.
CORS grants other sites permission to read responses: exact origin allowlist, never reflect the Origin header with credentials.
All three attack the browser's trust rules; fix them on the server and verify with tests.
Secrets do not belong in code, images or chat: inject them at run time and use a vault when you can.
Scan for secrets by format and entropy, in pre-commit and CI; wrap secrets so they cannot be printed by accident.
Rotate with an overlap window so old and new keys both work briefly.
A leaked secret is remediated by revoking it first; deleting or rewriting history only tidies up.
Your dependencies are your attack surface: pin versions, pin hashes, and upgrade deliberately with automated pull requests.
Typosquatting and dependency confusion abuse name lookup: check new names, and restrict private names to the private index.
Keep an SBOM so you can answer "do we use it?" in minutes when an advisory lands.
Compare versions with a real parser, not strings.
Least privilege limits blast radius: assume some piece will be compromised and make that piece powerless.
Containers: non-root, small pinned base, no baked secrets, read-only filesystem. Kubernetes: securityContext, no needless service-account token, default-deny NetworkPolicy.
IAM evaluates default deny, explicit deny wins, allow must match action and resource. Start narrow; give each service its own identity.
Linters catch the mechanical mistakes; review catches the design ones.

r: An SLI measures user experience as good events over valid events; an SLO is the target; an SLA is a contract with penalties.
The error budget is 1 minus the SLO. It makes reliability a number you can spend.
Burn rate (observed error rate divided by allowed rate) tells you how urgent a problem is.
Severity comes from customer impact and rules written in advance; adjust it as facts arrive.
On-call is a shared, scheduled duty with a primary, a secondary and an escalation path.
Pages must be urgent, actionable and about user impact. Everything else is a ticket or a dashboard.
Review the pager weekly: delete or demote alerts that do not lead to action.
On call you may act (roll back, flag off, page others) without asking permission, and asking for help early is a strength.
Six stages: detect, triage, mitigate, communicate (in parallel), resolve, learn.
Mitigate first with blunt tools (rollback, flag off, failover, shed load); understand later.
Measure time to detect, acknowledge, mitigate and resolve from timestamps, and say which "R" you mean.
Communicate on a fixed rhythm even when nothing changed, and verify recovery from the user's side.
Give each job one owner: incident commander, operations lead, communications lead and scribe.
The IC decides and coordinates; the IC does not debug. Only ops changes production.
Announce changes before and after doing them; keep one channel per incident.
Hand over the IC role after a few hours, out loud.
Debug with hypotheses: predict what you would see, check cheaply, write down the result.
First ask "what changed?", ranked by timing and by whether it touches the failing path.
RED (rate, errors, duration) for services; USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources.
Bisect large ranges: each test halves the search. Change one thing at a time.
Metrics say when it started, traces say where the time went, logs say why.
In logs, group by signature and read the earliest error from the lowest layer.
Use percentiles per minute, look for the step, and compare with the same time last week.
In traces, rank spans by self time; write every timestamp in UTC.
A runbook is a short, structured, linked-from-the-alert guide anyone can follow half asleep.
Because it is structured, you can lint it in CI: every alert has a complete, recently reviewed runbook.
Automate in rungs: written step, script, suggest-and-approve, guarded auto-remediation.
Guardrails: rate limits, blast-radius caps, dry runs, audit logs and an off switch.
Prepare templates: what is happening, who is affected, what we are doing, what we do not know, when next.
Status words (Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, Resolved) have fixed meanings.
Label guesses, avoid blame and the phrase "root cause" mid-incident, and keep your update promises.
Same facts, different framing for customers, support and leadership; close with an apology and a summary.
Blameless means we investigate systems and decisions in context, so that people report mistakes honestly.
Timelines use one clock (UTC) and facts only; merging sources shows the gaps that matter.
Use trigger, latent condition and contributing factors instead of a single root cause.
5 whys traps: stopping at a person, one linear chain, stopping early, invented certainty.
Action items: owner, due date, type, specific change, and a way to verify.
A good postmortem fits on a page or two: summary, numbers, one-clock timeline, causes, what went well/badly/lucky, actions.
Impact should be computed from data: failed requests, minutes, budget consumed.
The narrative names trigger, latent condition and contributing factors, not a person.
Actions cover prevent, detect and mitigate, each with owner, date and verification.
Three families of fixes: detect sooner (alerts), remember forever (regression tests), make it hard (guardrails).
Burn-rate alerts with a long and a short window page fast and reset fast.
Turn each incident into a failing-then-passing regression test of the requirement.
Canaries with automatic abort and validators in CI prevent, alerts merely shorten.
Review by risk: correctness, security, failure handling and data come before readability and style.
Risk depends on what is touched (auth, payments, migrations, config), not only on size.
Use a short checklist; automate style with a formatter and linter.
Comments are about the code, labelled by severity, explained, and kind; authors keep changes small and reply to everything.
A unified diff has files, hunk headers with line numbers, and lines marked +, - or space.
Scan only added lines, and track the new-file line number correctly.
Keep rules as data with an id, pattern, message and severity; keep patterns narrow to avoid false positives.
Test the rules with must-match and must-not-match lines; a checker helps review but never replaces it.
Reliability is bought, not free: compare options by expected loss avoided per unit cost.
Series multiplies availabilities (worse), parallel multiplies failure chances (better) but only when failures are independent.
Shared causes such as config, deploys and databases cap every replica; fix them first.
Let the error budget steer the balance between features and reliability, and decide per user journey.
